From the Utility Types page (all four sections in view):

1) Pick<Type, Keys>
- Generic signature (visible heading):
  - Pick<Type, Keys>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Keeps only the properties from Type whose keys are in Keys.
- First displayed example (Pick section):
  - Code (first part of the example block around `Pick`):
    - `interface Todo {`
    - `  title: string;`
    - `  description: string;`
    - `  completed: boolean;`
    - `}`
    - `type TodoPreview = Pick<Todo, "title" | "completed">;`
  - Result shown in the example block:
    - After the code, the docs’ inline evaluation shows the resulting type alias (in the same code block) as something equivalent to:
      - `type TodoPreview = { title: string; completed: boolean; }`
    - In words: `TodoPreview` contains only `title` and `completed` from `Todo`; `description` is removed.

2) Omit<Type, Keys>
- Generic signature (visible heading):
  - Omit<Type, Keys>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Removes the properties from Type whose keys are in Keys, keeping all the rest.
- First displayed example (Omit section):
  - Example code block begins:
    - `interface Todo {`
    - `  title: string;`
    - `  description: string;`
    - `  completed: boolean;`
    - `  createdAt: number;`
    - `}`
    - `type TodoPreview = Omit<Todo, "description">;`
    - `const todo: TodoPreview = {`
    - `  title: "Clean room",`
    - `  completed: false,`
    - `  createdAt: 1615544252770,`
    - `};`
    - `todo;`
    - (and then continues with `type TodoInfo = Omit<Todo, "completed" | ...` further down the same block)
  - Result shown for the first alias in that block:
    - The inline evaluation in the block shows (after the first alias) a type of the form:
      - `type TodoPreview = { title: string; completed: boolean; createdAt: number; }`
    - In words: `TodoPreview` keeps all keys of `Todo` except `description`; i.e., it removes `description` and keeps `title`, `completed`, and `createdAt`.

3) Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers>
- Generic signature (visible heading):
  - Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Removes from UnionType any union members that are assignable to ExcludedMembers; the remaining members are kept.
- First displayed example (Exclude section):
  - Example code block content at the top of the Exclude example:
    - `type T0 = Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">;`
    - followed immediately in the same block by its evaluated result:
      - `type T0 = "b" | "c"`
    - (the example then continues with other Exclude uses, but T0 is the first.)
  - Result of the first example:
    - `T0` is the union `"b" | "c"`.
    - In words: Exclude removed the member `"a"` from the original union `"a" | "b" | "c"`.

4) Extract<Type, Union>
- Generic signature (visible heading):
  - Extract<Type, Union>
- What it keeps/removes:
  - Keeps only those members of Type that are assignable to Union; all other union members are removed.
- First displayed example (Extract section):
  - Example code block content at the top of the Extract example:
    - `type T0 = Extract<"a" | "b" | "c", "a" | "f">;`
    - followed immediately in the same block by its evaluated result:
      - `type T0 = "a"`
    - (the example then continues with other `Extract` uses, but T0 is the first.)
  - Result of the first example:
    - `T0` is the union `"a"`.
    - In words: Extract kept only the overlapping member `"a"` between `"a" | "b" | "c"` and `"a" | "f"` and removed all others.

Relation of keyof to Pick and Omit (from the Handbook > Keyof Type Operator page examples):
- On the `keyof` type operator page (navigated via Handbook → Keyof Type Operator):
  - The examples show that `keyof T` produces a union of the property names (as string or symbol literals) of object type `T`.
  - For example, one of the early examples has an object type with certain properties and shows:
    - `type P = keyof T;`
    - and P evaluates to a union of those property names.
- How this relates to Pick and Omit:
  - Pick<Type, Keys>:
    - The Keys parameter is constrained (conceptually and in practice) to be a subtype of `keyof Type`—i.e., it must be made up of valid property names of Type.
    - The examples on the Pick utility type page use literal unions like `"title" | "completed"` in the Keys position; on the keyof page you see how such unions can be *derived* from a type via `keyof`. Combining these ideas, you can write things like `Pick<T, K>` where `K extends keyof T`, ensuring only existing keys are selected.
  - Omit<Type, Keys>:
    - Omit is defined in terms of Pick and Exclude in the language design, roughly as:
      - `type Omit<T, K extends keyof any> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;`
    - The keyof page’s examples clarify that `keyof T` gives all keys of T; then Exclude removes the unwanted keys, and Pick selects the remaining ones. The Omit examples on the Utility Types page (like omitting "description") illustrate the resulting behavior.
  - Conceptual linkage from the examples:
    - `keyof` provides the *set of keys* available on a type, represented as a union.
    - Pick uses a subset of that union (Keys) to keep only those properties.
    - Omit effectively uses `keyof` plus `Exclude` to remove some of those keys and then Pick the remainder.

So, according to the visible examples:
- keyof takes an object type and returns a union of its keys.
- Pick takes an object type and a union of keys (compatible with `keyof` of that type) and keeps just those keys.
- Omit uses the same key space (given by `keyof`) and removes the keys listed, which the docs’ examples illustrate by showing the resulting types with only the expected remaining properties.
